author: Cunningham
note: Udyana people's language and Fa-Hian's three-day hospitality custom; Takka tribe and Attak; no location of a Xiyu ji place

author: Cunningham
note: Takka-desa and the Takkas; Fa-Hian footnote only

author: Cunningham
note: Gakars: both pilgrims avoided their country; no location

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: Balmer (W Rajputana)
quote: At this very period also, as we learn from Hwen Thsang, the capital of Guryjara was named Balamer
note: passing statement in the Bala/Kathi discussion; same as AG (Pi-lo-mi-lo = Balmer); Mizutani (majority) Bhinmal

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: between the Chenab and the Ravi
quote: the itinerary of the Chinese pilgrim Hwen Thsang shows most decisively that the Séhala of the Hindus was situated between the Chendb and the Ravi
note: Fa-Hian's crossing of the Jhelam at Bhera (Faxian-only) in same passage; Sakala W of the Ravi as AG; Mizutani Sialkot

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: rocky hill of Sangala, W of the Ravi
quote: I necd only mention here that the rocky hill of Sangala still exists, and that it is to the westward of the Ravi, in the very position
note: same as AG (Sanglawala-Tiba); Mizutani Sialkot

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: new capital Tse-kia, kingdom from the Indus to the Bias
quote: the old city of Sikala had been deserted for many centuries, and the new city, which he calls Zse-Kia, was then the capital…of alarge kingdom which extended from the Indus to the Byas
note: extent as AG; mainly a discussion of the reading tse = cerebral ta

author: Cunningham
note: reading of the name Tse-kia (Taka or Kata); no location

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: Balmer, half way between Amarkot and Jodhpur
quote: These princes I would refer to the Gurjjara kingdom of Hwen Thsang, of which the capital in his time was Pilomalo, or Balmer, half way between Amarkot and Jodhpur.
note: same as AG (Balmer); Mizutani Bhinmal; in the Gujar/Yuchi discussion

author: Cunningham
note: Kshatriya king of Kabul; political history

author: Cunningham
note: Tochari script and coins of Kapisa/Bamiyan; no location

author: Cunningham
note: introduction to the Panjab antiquities

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: ruins E of Shah-dheri, 10 miles SE of Hasan Abdal
evidence: site found by Cunningham in 1863 (against Vivien's Usman-Katar)
quote: the actual emplacement, which I have discovered during the present year, being to the east of Shah-dheri, at 10 miles to the South-East of Hasan-Abdal, and 4 miles to the South of Usmin-Katar.
note: same as AG and Mizutani (Taxila); also a summary of Xuanzang's Panjab itinerary

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: Peshawar; Kanishka monastery = Gor-Katri; Pushkalavati = Parang and Charsada (Hashtnagar); two stupas = Tarangzai and Tangi; Varusha = Palodheri; Dantaloka = Kashmiri-ghar cave hill
evidence: Kashmiri-ghar cave 3-4 miles ENE of Palodheri; inscription copied there 1848; Pushkalavati distance read 100 li (Life) not 50
quote: I believe that this great monastery was still existing in the times of Baber and Akbar under the name of Gor-Katari…The full distance of 16 miles will bring us to the two large towns of Parang and Charsada…These two places are probably represented by Tarangzai and Tangi…These conditions are best fulfilled by the village of Palodheri
note: Varusha at Palodheri differs from Mizutani (Shahbaz Garhi); Tarangzai/Tangi for 02.04.12/13 where Mizutani has no identification; otherwise as AG

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: Karamar hill (bearing read SE); Ohind on the Indus
evidence: Karamar 3,480 ft, 8 miles SE of Palodheri
quote: there is a very lofty mountain called Kdramdr, 3,480 feet in height, which is exactly 8 miles to the south-east of Palo-dheri…tallies exactly with the position of Ohind, which is situated on the north bank of the Indus, 15 miles above Attak
note: Karamar agrees with Mizutani; Ohind as AG and Mizutani

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: Ohind (Waihand)
evidence: name history from Abu Rihan, Rashid-ud-din, Ferishta (Bithanda)
quote: From all these examples, I infer that the original name of Utakhanda, or Ut-khand, was first softened to Uthand or Bithanda, and then shortened to Uhand or Ohind.
note: rejects Loewenthal's Attak

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: Ohind
evidence: Indus has carried away half the town; gold-washers' finds: bronze buckles, ornaments, Indo-Scythian and Brahman Kabul coins
quote: the gold-washers find numerous coins and atrinkets, which offer the best evidence of the former prosperity of the city.

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: Lahor, 4 miles NE of Ohind
evidence: Greek and Indo-Scythian coins obtained at Lahor 1848
quote: From the bearing and distance there can be no hesitation in identifying Sddtura with the small modern town of Lahor, which is exactly 4 miles to the north-east of Ohind.
note: text bearing NW but site NE of Ohind, not discussed; as AG and Mizutani

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: Mahaban mountain (Bunir); Musura = Sura in the Chumla valley
quote: the Mahavana Hill was visited by Ilwen Thsang in A. D. 630…This place may, I believe, to identified with the large village of Sura, in the Chumla valley, which is just 10 miles to the north-west of the highest peak of Mahdban.
note: quote just before the passage (the hit is its footnote); in the Aornos argument; as AG; Mizutani Shinasi stupa / Gogdara

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: Hashtnagar
quote: has been fixed beyond all doubt at Hashtnagar by the concurrent testimony of the Chinese pilgrims.
note: Aornos/Embolima discussion

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: ruins near Shah-dheri, 1 mile NE of Kala-ka-sarai
evidence: three marches from the Indus as in Mughal and modern stages
quote: But the itineraries of the Chinese pilgrims agree in placing it at three days’ journey to the east of the Indus, or in the immediate…just one mile to the north-east of Kéla-ka-sarai
note: as AG and Mizutani

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: 3 days E/SE of the Indus
quote: Sungyun also places it three days to the cast of tho Indus (Beal’s Translation, p. 200), and Hwen,Thsang three days to the south-east.
note: footnote on the pilgrims' distances

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: N of the city: Babar Khana land ('tiger's house'); district Chach-Hazara = Sirsha-sahasra
evidence: local names Babar Khana and Chach-Hazara
quote: At 12 or-18 @¢ or 2 miles to the north of the-city there was a stupa of King Asoka…the land immediately to the north of the ruined city is still called Babar Khana
note: name-based; see 141 for the stupa itself

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: Bir mound; head-gift stupa 2 miles N in Babarkhana
evidence: great ruined stupa 8,000 ft NNE of the Bir mound; Hatial fort measured; tower excavated to 26 ft
quote: Judging from the size of the place, I take it to be the site of the inhabited part of the city in the time of wen Thsang…I think there can be little doubt that the city of his time was situated on the mound of Bir.
note: Bir mound as AG; differs from Mizutani (Sirsukh)

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: great stupa on the Lundi river 1,200 ft beyond Jhandiala Pind (Babar-khana)
evidence: main road of Sirkap runs due N to it; Seri-ki-pind mound ('head-gift' name) 3,600 ft NW; Sir-Sukh measured
quote: a large stupa on the bank of the Lundi River, 1,200 feet beyond the Jhandidla Pind. This I believe to be the famous head-gift. stupa…I think that there are very strong grounds for identifying the great ruined tope of Babar-khdéna with the famous stwpa of the
note: as AG; differs from Mizutani (Bhallar stupa, Marshall)

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: Shah-dheri ruins (Sirkap, Sir-Sukh etc.)
evidence: irrigated land N of the Tabra Nala from the Haro river fits the springs and water-courses
quote: This then must be the site of Taxila, which, according to the unanimous testimony of ancient writers, was the largest city between the Indus and Hydaspes.

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: spring of Baba-Wali (Panja Sahib), Hasan Abdal
evidence: Hasan Abdal 10-11 miles NW of Shah-dheri; spring and tank visited 1848 and 1864
quote: Both the direction and distance of the Chinese pilgrim point to Hasan Abdal, which bears north-west 10 miles distant from Shah-dheri by the new main road
note: agrees with Mizutani; AG column empty for this site

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: Baba-Wali spring, Hasan Abdal
evidence: local legend (Sikh, Muhammadan versions)
quote: In the time of Hwen Thsang, A. D. 630, the legend of the place referred to the Ndga or Serpent King of the fountain, named Zldpatra.

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: Hasan Abdal spring
evidence: Sikh legend read as a Buddhist original; ruined monastery 200 ft square and stupa near the cypress garden; half a Greco-Bactrian coin; old name Haro
quote: its evident connection with the legend of Hwen Thsang is a most satisfactory proof of the identity of the clear spring of ITasan Abdal with the Naga fountain of the Chinese pilgrim…On this mound I traced the ruins of a monastery, 200 feet square, and of a large stupa

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: Baoti Pind (bearing read E for SE)
evidence: ruins of a large town; Langar-kot / Srikot fort in the gorge
quote: The distance points to the neighbourhood of Baoti Pind, where I found the ruins of a large town and of several Buddhist monuments. But the bearing is east
note: agrees with Mizutani

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: stupa on the NE peak of the Baoti ridge
evidence: stupa 65 ft diam. on a platform with monastery 70 x 58 ft; excavated: relic chamber at 8 ft, earthenware vessel
quote: I judged that it might possibly be the actual stupa which was said to have been built by Asoka…At 8 feet from the top my excavation came upon a small chamber, 2 feet square

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: chief tope of Kurmal, on a N spur of the Margala range SE of the Bir mound
evidence: tope 50 ft diam. excavated to rock (no deposit); monastery 120 ft square; name Kurmal ~ Kunala
quote: The position of the chief tope of Kurmal tallies, therefore, so exactly with the site of Kundla Stupa as described by Hwen Thsang, that I have but little hésitation in proposing their identity.
note: Mizutani: Marshall's site on the N slope of the Hathial ridge (disputed); AG column empty

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: Manikyala: General Court's stupa ('Sin-tu' read as the Suhan river)
evidence: 200 li SE of Taxila = Manikyala; Court's inscription twice names the huta-murtta; red soil
quote: which is the exact bearing and distance of Maniky4la from the ruined city near Shah-dheri…This I believe to have been the great stwpa which was successfully explored by General Court.
note: as AG; differs from Mizutani (Banj mountain, Buner, across the Indus)

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: Manikyala
evidence: Rasalu legend compared with the tiger-cub jataka
quote: the great capital of Manikpur was the ideal creation of the fabulist to give reality to the tradition
note: legend argument only

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: Court's topes Nos. 2 and 5, Manikyala
evidence: burnt monastery N of Court's tope excavated
quote: These two stupas I propose to identify with General Court’s topes, Nos. 2 and 5
note: 03.04.06 (stone stupa near the body-offering site) = No. 5 'blood-offering'; Mizutani: existence unknown

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: Court's No. 2 (body) and No. 5, 1,200 ft S (blood)
evidence: relative positions; red soil; inscription huta-murtti; deposit of Kanishka gold, Roman denarii, Kushan copper
quote: The latter stupa I would identify with General Court’s No. 5, a ruin of considerable size, which is situated just 1,200 feet to the south of No. 2

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: ruined gateway ESE of Court's tope
evidence: excavated foundations of a courtyard with 12-ft passage
quote: I think that it may have been the stone gate-way through which Hwen Thsang passed on his visit to the stupa of the body-oblation.
note: bearing ESE instead of S

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: Ventura's great tope post-dates Xuanzang
evidence: Sassano-Arabian coins at 64 ft inside the great tope
quote: we can only conclude that Hwen Thsang’s silence is due to the non-existence of the tope at the period of his visit in A. D. 680.
note: rules out the great tope as the body-offering stupa

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: Sinhapura = Malot (Salt Range); ten tanks = pools of the Ganiya Nala below Katas; Sakala = Sangala hill; Tse-kia = Asarur
evidence: Sangala hill surveyed: triangle, N side 215 ft high, base c.1 mile round, bricks 15x9x3 in.; Asarur 112 miles from both Rajaori and Jalandhar
quote: I think, however, that Malot must be the Sinhapura of Hwen Thsang…The ten holy tanks I would identify with the different pools in the bed of-the Ganiya Nala below Katds…I found the ruins of a large town, called Asarwr
note: Sinhapura at Malot is the 1863-64 view, later given up: AG and Mizutani have Ketas (city = Kotera); Jayapura of the Life = probably Hafizabad

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: Sangala hill; Asoka stupa = Mundapapura ridge NW
evidence: brick ruins c.1.5 miles round; robbers in the Pilu forest (Po-lo-she read Pi-lo); Apaga = Ayak Nadi
quote: This I would identify with the low ridge of rock on the north-west called Mundapapura…In November 1863 I approached Sakala from the east through a continuous wood of Pélu trees
note: new: Asoka stupa 5-6 li NW of the monastery in Sakala; Mizutani Sialkot

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: capital of the Takka kingdom
quote: the neighbouring town of TZse-kia as the capital of a large kingdom, which extended from the Indus to the Bids

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: W of the Ravi
quote: But the detailed measurements of Hwen Thsang are too precise, the statement of the Mahabharata is too clear, and the coincidence of name is too exact to be set aside lightly.
note: against Arrian/Curtius placing Sangala E of the Ravi

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: Asarur, 45 miles from Lahore
quote: Hwen Thsang’s Zse-kia, which was the capital of the Panjab in A. D. 633…It is 19 miles distant from Sangala by the road, but not more than 16 miles in a direct line across the country.
note: as AG (Asarur); Mizutani: capital perhaps new Sakala

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: Asarur; Asoka stupa = mound of Sdier near Thata Syadon; Nara-Sinha = Ran-si mound
evidence: Asarur ruins 15,600 ft round; 15 li read 115 li; moulded and wedge-shaped bricks; Ran-si mound 600 x 500 ft with large bricks and coins
quote: The circuit of Tse-kia was about 20 , or upwards of 3 miles, which agrees sufficiently well with my measurement of the ruins of Asarur at 15,600 feet…This stupa may, I think, be identified with the little mound of Sdiér near Thata Syadon
note: new: Asoka stupa c.10 li NE of the capital; Nara-Sinha (Ran-si) is from the Life only

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: Thanesar; Kurukshetra between the Saraswati and Drishadwati
quote: the earliest certain notice of it under this name is by the Chinese pilgrim Hwen Thsang in A. D. 634…All the country immediately around Thanesar, between the Saraswati and Drishadwati Rivers, is known by the name of Kuru-Kshetra

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: Kurukshetra circuit
evidence: modern pilgrimage circuit 48 kos; reads 400 li for 200
quote: is also called Dharma-Kshetra, or the…which is evidently the orginal of Hwen Thsang’s…Iam myself quite satisfied of the necessity for making this correction in the pilgrim’s number

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: holy land extending to the Drishadwati
evidence: Sanskrit texts (Vamana Purana, Mahabharata, Manu)
quote: From these texts it is certain that the holy land of Kurukshetra must have extended to the Drishadwati in the time of Hwen Thsang, and therefore that his limitation of its circuit to 200 li, or 20 kos, moust be erroneous.

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: plain W of Thanesar towards Aujasghat
evidence: local tradition points out the site; lake measured 3,546 x 1,900 ft
quote: All my enquiries for them were fruitless, but the site of Asthipur is still pointed out in the plain to the west of the city towards Aujasghat.
note: as AG and Mizutani

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: Thanesar fort, town and Bahari; stupa = Madrasa mound NW
evidence: mounds 14,000 ft round, c.4 miles with the Darra; reddish-yellow bricks on the Madrasa mound
quote: Taking in this space, the original city would have been as nearly as possible an exact square of one mile on each side, which would give a circuit of 4 miles…In the position here indicated I found two ruined mounds
note: new: Asoka brick stupa 4-5 li NW of the city

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: Gokantha = Gunana, 17 miles SSW of Thanesar; Srughna = Sugh
evidence: Sugh on a spur in a bend of the old Jumna (W Jumna canal); 55 miles from Gunana
quote: The village of Gundna between Vyasthali and Nisang, and 17 miles to the south south-west of Thanesar, appears to agree very well with the recorded position…In speaking of this place in my last year’s report, I stated my opinion that it ought to be looked for somewhere in the neighbourhood of K/dils…I found a village named Sugh
note: revises his ASR I view (near Kalsi); as AG (Sugh, Gunana tentative); Sugh agrees with Mizutani

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: Sugh, Mandalpur, Dyalgarh, Buriya
evidence: three forts; circuit 22,000 ft, 19,000 without the N fort
quote: This would reduce the circuit of the position to 19,000 feet, or upwards of 34 miles, and bring it into accord with the pilgrim’s measurement.

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: Mandal = later name of Srughna; Madawar near Bijnor; Mayura = Mayapur
evidence: marched Sugh-Haridwar: 65 miles; reads 400 li for 800
quote: which I have already identified with Mad&war or Mandéwar, 9 miles to the north of Bijuor in Rohilkhand…I feel satisfied, therefore, that Hwen Thsang’s recorded distance of 800 i, or 1333 miles, has by some mistake been doubled
note: Madawar as AG; Mizutani: region E of the Ganges opposite Srughna

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: Mayapur, old ruined town between Haridwar and Kankhal
evidence: local name Mayapur
quote: the old ruined town between Haridwir and Kankhal is…still ealled Wdydpur
note: as AG and Mizutani

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: Brahma-kund well at the Gangadwara temple, Haridwar
quote: Close by in a small temple is a well called Brahmd-kund, which is most probably the same that was noticed by Hwen Thsang in A. D. 634

author: Cunningham
note: Ganges bathing belief (Mahabhadra); no location

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: Bairat, capital of Matsya
evidence: Abu Rihan's Narana = Narayanpur 10 miles NE of Bairat
quote: The bearing and distance from Mathura point unequivocally to Bairdi, the ancient capital of Ifatsya, as the city of Uwen Thsang’s narrative
note: Report 1864-65; cites Ancient Geography p.144; as AG and Mizutani

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: Bairat mound
evidence: mound size matches 14-15 li; Asoka inscription on a hill 1 mile SW
quote: According to him, the capital was 14 or 15 Ui, or just 24 miles, in circuit, which corresponds almost exactly with the size of the ancient mound on which the present town is built.

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: ruins on the Bijak hill = two of the eight monasteries
evidence: platforms with monks' cells; Asoka inscription (Buddhist) found there; early cast copper coins
quote: These ruins on the Bijak hillI take to be the remains of two of the eight Buddhist monasteries, which were still in existence at the time of Hwen Thsang’s visit

author: Cunningham
note: Bairat king's caste Fei-she; no location

author: Cunningham
note: Harsha's rule; Narwar history

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: Bundelkhand; capital Mahoba or Khajuraho
evidence: distribution of the Jajhotiya Brahmans; reads ~2000 li from Ujain
quote: He calls it Chi-chi-to, or Jajhoti, and places the capital at 1,000 , or 167 miles, to the north-east of Ujain…it is evident that the province of Jajhoti corresponded with the modern district of Bundelkhand, in its widest extent.
note: Report 1864-65; as AG; Mizutani undecided (Bundelkhand or Chitor)

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: Khajuraho: Ganthai temple and mound No. 28
evidence: pedestal with 'Ye dharmma hetu' (6th-7th c.); monastery cells traced on mound 28
quote: There are no traditions whatever, and the only remains that I can attribute with any certainty to this period are a single pillared temple, No. 21, called Ganthai, and a high mound, No. 28, which is most probably a ruined monastery.

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: Khajuraho (rather than Mahoba)
evidence: ruins 4,500 x 2,500 ft, circuit 14,000 ft = Xuanzang's 15-16 li
quote: This corresponds almost exactly with the size of the capital as recorded by Hwen Thsang in A. D 641…I think it most probable that Khajurtho must have been the capital of the earlier dynasty of Jajhotiya Brahmans.
note: AG keeps Mahoba as alternative; Mizutani undecided

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: northern group of mounds at Khajuraho (Satdhara etc.)
evidence: mound No. 15 (Satdhara) 200 x 150 ft with lintels and stone elephants
quote: The northern group, which is situated at an average distance of three-quarters of a mile from the western group, consists chiefly of ruined mounds, which are very probably the remains of the numerous Buddhist monasteries

author: Cunningham

evidence: Katra has hollows 25-30 ft deep and mounds to the N; jail mound has a tank and Buddhist remains
quote: In my Report of 1862-63 I identified the Katra and jail mounds with the two principal Buddhist establishments described by the Chinese pilgrim Hwen Thsang…the jail mound is the actual site of the place described by
note: Upagupta site hedged (Katra preferred; bearing E read W); Mizutani: cannot be located; new: the dry tank where the monkey offered honey (24-25 li SE)

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: Masar, not Buxar
evidence: visited Buxar: Brahmanical site, no antiquities
quote: I have, however, now visited both Buxar and Masdér, and Iam quite convinced that the latter is the true representative of Hwen Thsang’s Malhdsdra

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: Masar, 6 miles W of Ara
evidence: seven Jain inscriptions (S.1443/1448) name the place Mahasara; no Buddhist trace; Banasur statue

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: Masar on the old bed of the Ganges; Desert monastery near Bhojpur
evidence: old Ganges channels (Ganga, Gangi) past Bihiya, Masar and Ara
quote: it stands upon the high bank of the old bed of the Ganges…But the two distances of 10 and 12 yojanae point to the neighbourhood of Bhojpur as the actual position of the

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: Masar
evidence: inscriptions of S.1448 naming Raja Natha Deva of Mahasara
quote: in the reign of Raja Nitha Deva, of Mahas4ra, under the teacher Kamala Kirtti

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: Masar town c.1 x 0.5 mile; Ara
evidence: extent of mounds; demon stupa first linked to Ara (aranya)
quote: the old town of Mahdsdra must have been nearly one mile in length from east to west, by half a milo in width…Before I visited Ara I had a vague impression that the namp of the place might have some connection with dranya

author: Cunningham
name_in_asr: Narayana temple; stupa of the 'demons of the desert'
asr_identification: temple on the N bank opposite Masar; demon stupa = Ara
evidence: Ara legend of the man-eating Asur Baka killed by Bhima
quote: I suppose that the temple stood on the opposit2 bank of the Ganger within sight of Mahdsara…and are able to conduct him to Arf, whose exist

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: Ara (Ekachakra)
evidence: Mahabharata Baka legend

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: Bitha mound, 16 miles E of Ara (bearing read NE)
evidence: yojana of 40 li = 7 miles from Banaras-Vaisali sums
quote: According to the text, Hwen Thsang travelled 100 4, or 17 miles, to the south-east, for which I propose to read north-east…There is bower a place called Bitha, or “the mound” just 16 miles to the east, which may very probably turn out to be the ruins of the Drona Stupa.
note: revises AG (Deghwara near Chapra); Mizutani unknown; 07.03 removed (only sums distances)

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: Bodh Gaya: Bodhi tree terrace; great temple = Xuanzang's vihara
evidence: temple base 47'3" x 48'8", height 160 ft; brick sizes show later E additions
quote: This is, I think, beyond all doubt the same Vikdr that was seen and described by Hwen Thsang, as the two agree in several minute rticulars, as well as in the essential point of size.
note: new: the Vajrasana (diamond throne) on the Bodhimanda; as AG and Mizutani

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: Bodh Gaya temple sanctum
evidence: wall thicknesses read against the Sasanka/minister story
quote: There is a curious story told by Hwen Thsang, to which the long shape of this cell of the great temple seems to lend an air of tru

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: ruined walls and staircases on the E front of the temple
quote: These remains answer so well to the descrip

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: Budhain hill; bambu forest Jakhtiban near Jethian; Tapoban springs
evidence: bambus still cut on the hill; no Asoka stupa or cave found
quote: which I have already identified with the Budhain mountain, one of the stations of the Indian survey…a place called Tapoban, or simply Tapo, one mile and three quarters from the village of Jethian
note: Buddhavana Budhain differs from Mizutani (no accepted identification)

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: cave behind Jarasandh-ki-baithak (NE slope of Baibhar); Son-bhandar cave
evidence: cave found and cleared Jan 1872, 40 ft long; baithak 85 ft square 289 ft from the stream; caves 3,000 ft apart
quote: This, then, was the Pippal cave, or Vaibheva cave, of the Chinese pilgrims, in which Buddha had actually dwelt and taken his meals…The Son-bhdnddr cave was therefore beyond all doubt the famous Suttapani cave of the Buddhists
note: revises AG (Pippala at Ratnagiri; Son Bhandar only 'perhaps'); Pippala close to Mizutani's N-face cave

author: Cunningham

author: Cunningham

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: Giryek hill; Hamsa monastery on the lower E peak
